Our Roorkee · Thomason College to IIT Roorkee

A canal, a college, and 154 years to 2001

1842

A village on the Solani

Roorkee was still a village on the banks of the Solani river when digging began on Colonel Proby Cautley's Ganga Canal in April 1842. The canal was the largest irrigation work of its age, and it needed engineers. India had nowhere to train them.

The Solani Aqueduct, which carries the canal past Roorkee, photographed in the 1860s. Rijksmuseum, public domain.
1847

A college is proposed

On 23 September 1847 James Thomason, Lieutenant-Governor of the North-Western Provinces, proposed an engineering college at Roorkee. The government notification followed on 25 November 1847, and classes began on 1 January 1848 under the first Principal, R. Maclagan. It was the first engineering college in India.

James Thomason (1804–1853). Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
1854

The canal opens, the college takes a name

The Ganga Canal formally opened on 8 April 1854. Thomason had died the previous autumn, and the Roorkee College was renamed the Thomason College of Civil Engineering in his memory. The stone lions on the canal at Roorkee date from this era.

The Ganges Canal at Roorkee, watercolour by William Simpson, 1863. Public domain.
1860s–1890s

Thomason College grows up

The college was affiliated to Calcutta University in 1864 and to Allahabad in 1894. Football arrived in 1872, polo and hockey soon after, swimming in 1890. In 1896 Bir Shamsher of Nepal presented the clock that still sits on the dome. In 1897 the course grew to three years and Electrical Engineering was added; electricity itself reached the college in 1898.

The Thomason Civil Engineering College, photographed in the 1860s. Rijksmuseum, public domain.
1949

University of Roorkee

Independent India needed engineers of its own. The Roorkee University Act of 1947 raised the college to a university, and on 25 November 1949, a hundred years after the founding notification, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru presented the charter of the University of Roorkee, the first engineering university of independent India.

The Main Building, renamed the James Thomason Building in 2015. Photo: Fowler&fowler, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
1982

Thomso

The first Thomso, the university's cultural festival, was held in 1982. By our time it was the week the whole campus lived for. Thomso '98: the future happens.

Thomso '98, from Ankur Gupta's album.
1997

150 years, and we walk in

The University marked its 150th year from October 1996, and India Post issued a commemorative stamp in 1997. That same year our batch came in through the gate. The place we joined was a century and a half old and about to change its name again.

India Post commemorative stamp, 1997. Government Open Data License, India.
2001

From UOR to IITR

We graduated in the summer of 2001. On 21 September 2001 the University of Roorkee became the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the country's seventh IIT. Dr D. V. Singh, the last Vice-Chancellor, became the first Director. We came in through the gates of the University of Roorkee and walked out as the first batch of IIT Roorkee, carrying the legacy and spirit of UOR with us. This is where the carousel stops.

The sign at the gate today. Photo: Ravi Dwivedi, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Since then: the Main Building became the James Thomason Building in 2015, and in 2022 the institute turned 175.
